articles.surfaceLabel: Does Argentina's Privacy Law Apply to Your Organization?
articles.plainSummary: Argentina has protected personal data since 2000, rooted in a constitutional right called habeas data. The law applies to personal data recorded in files and databases in Argentina, in both the private and public sectors.
articles.personalImpact: In Argentina, control over your own data is rooted in the constitution as habeas data. Yet your details still fill credit databases and marketing lists. This law covers files and databases holding personal data in Argentina. It turns that constitutional promise into everyday rules.
articles.professionalLayer: Law 25,326 is one of Latin America's oldest comprehensive data protection laws, implementing the constitutional habeas data guarantee. It applies to personal data recorded in public and private files, registers, and databases within Argentina. The Agency for Access to Public Information supervises compliance. Argentina holds an EU adequacy decision dating from 2003, one of the earliest granted. The law predates the GDPR era, and its database-registration model and shorter response deadlines reflect that earlier generation. Modernization bills aligning Argentina more closely with GDPR have been introduced repeatedly but not yet enacted, so the 2000 framework remains the binding law.
articles.assessTrigger: Do you maintain databases containing personal data of people in Argentina, and are those databases registered with the AAIP as the law requires?

gapRemediation.smb: Confirm whether database registration applies to you. It is an obligation with no GDPR equivalent that foreign organizations often miss.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Assign ownership for AAIP registration and monitor the recurring modernization bills, which would materially change obligations if enacted.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Track Argentina within your Latin America program with local counsel, since practice relies heavily on AAIP dispositions layered over the 2000 statute.

comparisonFlags.note: Argentina requires registration of databases with the regulator, a pre-GDPR model the EU abandoned.

articles.surfaceLabel: Why Organizations Are Allowed to Use Your Data in Argentina
articles.plainSummary: Argentine law treats your consent as the general rule for using personal data. Consent must be free, express, and informed, and given in writing or by an equivalent means, with limited exceptions.
articles.personalImpact: Companies often gather your data far beyond what a service really needs. Argentine law says they need your informed consent, or another lawful reason, first. That consent must be clear, not buried in fine print. Collection without a valid basis is not permitted.
articles.professionalLayer: Article 5 establishes consent as the default requirement for lawful processing: free, express, and informed, documented in writing or equivalent form. Exceptions cover data from unrestricted public sources, data collected for state functions, limited basic listing data such as name and tax identification, obligations arising from contractual or professional relationships, and financial-sector operations under specific rules. Sensitive data receives stricter treatment, and no one can be compelled to disclose it. The framework is consent-centric in the pre-GDPR style rather than offering a menu of co-equal legal bases, with no legitimate-interests basis in the statute.
articles.assessTrigger: Does your Argentine processing rest on express informed consent or a statutory exception, given the law has no legitimate-interests basis to fall back on?

gapRemediation.smb: Collect express consent at intake. Do not assume GDPR-style legitimate interests reasoning transfers to Argentina.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Audit activities you justify by legitimate interests elsewhere. In Argentina they need consent or a listed exception.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Configure consent management to treat Argentina as consent-first, and document reliance on each statutory exception.

comparisonFlags.note: Argentina is consent-centric with no legitimate-interests basis. GDPR offers six co-equal bases.

articles.surfaceLabel: Your Right to See Your Data in Argentina
articles.plainSummary: You can ask any database holder whether it holds information about you and receive a copy. The organization must answer within 10 calendar days, one of the shortest access deadlines anywhere.
articles.personalImpact: Credit bureaus behind a Veraz report can decide your loans and rentals. The data driving that score is often invisible to you. This right lets you ask any database what it holds about you. A hidden file becomes something you can inspect.
articles.professionalLayer: Article 14 grants the right of access to personal data held in public or private databases, exercisable free of charge at intervals of six months unless a legitimate interest justifies more frequent requests. The information must be provided within 10 calendar days of the request. If the deadline passes or the answer is unsatisfactory, the constitutional habeas data action becomes available, giving the right unusual judicial teeth. Responses must be clear, complete, and cover the whole record held on the person.
articles.assessTrigger: Can your organization turn around Argentine access requests in 10 calendar days, well inside the one-month window your GDPR workflow assumes?

gapRemediation.smb: Flag Argentine requests for immediate handling. The 10-day clock leaves no room for a queue.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Configure your DSR tooling with a jurisdiction-specific SLA for Argentina rather than a global 30-day default.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Automate data retrieval for Argentine records so the 10-day statutory deadline is routinely achievable and audited.

comparisonFlags.note: Argentina requires access responses in 10 calendar days. GDPR allows one month.

articles.surfaceLabel: Your Right to Correct or Delete Your Data in Argentina
articles.plainSummary: You can demand that wrong, incomplete, or unlawfully held information about you be corrected, updated, or deleted. The organization must act within five business days.
articles.personalImpact: A wrong entry in a credit or marketing database can quietly close doors. It may deny you financing or a plan, with no explanation. This law lets you correct or remove inaccurate data. Decisions about you then rest on the truth.
articles.professionalLayer: Article 16 obliges the database controller to rectify, update, suppress, or subject to confidentiality the personal data of the requester within five business days of the claim or of detecting the error. During verification the controller must either block the record or annotate that its accuracy is contested. Onward correction flows to recipients of the data are required. As with access, failure opens the habeas data route. The five-business-day deadline is among the world's shortest for rectification and deletion.
articles.assessTrigger: Can you correct or delete Argentine records within five business days, including notifying downstream recipients of the change?

gapRemediation.smb: Treat correction and deletion requests as same-week work. Keep a recipient log so onward notification is possible.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Build the five-day SLA into the workflow and pre-map which systems must change for a single record.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Automate propagation of corrections across systems and to recipients, with completion logging against the five-day clock.

articles.surfaceLabel: What Happens When Your Data Is Compromised in Argentina
articles.plainSummary: Argentina's 2000 law does not contain a mandatory breach notification duty. The regulator recommends reporting incidents and keeping records, and modernization bills would make notification mandatory.
articles.personalImpact: A leak can expose your DNI number and financial records to fraudsters. Delay or silence from a company makes it worse. Argentine guidance calls for prompt notice to the AAIP and affected people. You are alerted in time to guard your identity.
articles.professionalLayer: Law 25,326 predates breach notification as a standard feature and imposes only general security obligations. AAIP Resolution 47/2018 recommends, as part of its recommended security measures, that incidents be documented and reported to the AAIP, and notification is treated as good practice evidencing compliance rather than a hard statutory duty. Sectoral rules may impose their own incident duties. Pending modernization bills would introduce a mandatory notification regime aligned with international practice, so this is an area to monitor closely.
articles.responseTimeline: No mandatory statutory deadline. Prompt voluntary reporting to the AAIP is recommended practice.
articles.assessTrigger: Does your incident plan cover Argentina with documented handling and voluntary AAIP reporting, and are you monitoring the modernization bills that would make notification mandatory?

gapRemediation.smb: Document incidents affecting Argentine data even without a legal duty. It is cheap insurance and expected practice.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Fold Argentina into your global incident process at your strictest standard rather than maintaining a weaker local path.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Apply your global notification standard to Argentina and track the pending bill as a horizon risk.

comparisonFlags.note: Argentina has no mandatory breach notification duty in the current statute. GDPR requires 72-hour notification.

articles.surfaceLabel: Moving Personal Data Out of Argentina
articles.plainSummary: Transfers to countries without adequate protection are prohibited unless an exception applies, such as the person's consent or approved contract clauses. The regulator publishes model clauses.
articles.personalImpact: Your data may be sent to companies in other countries. Some of them offer weaker protection than Argentina. This law allows the transfer only with adequate safeguards or your consent. Your protections do not end at the border.
articles.professionalLayer: Article 12 prohibits transfers to countries or international bodies that do not provide adequate levels of protection, subject to exceptions including consent, international judicial cooperation, medical emergencies, banking transfers, and treaty obligations. The AAIP maintains a list of jurisdictions it deems adequate, broadly tracking the EU adequacy map, and has approved model contractual clauses for transfers to non-adequate destinations. Argentina itself holds EU adequacy, keeping EU-to-Argentina flows unrestricted, a status tied to maintaining its protection standards.
articles.assessTrigger: Do your transfers out of Argentina rely on the AAIP adequacy list or its model clauses, rather than EU paperwork assumed to carry over?

gapRemediation.smb: Check your main vendors' locations against the AAIP adequacy list and add AAIP model clauses where needed.
gapRemediation.midMarket: Inventory Argentine-origin flows and attach the correct AAIP instrument to each.
gapRemediation.enterprise: Manage Argentine transfer paperwork within your regional program and monitor AAIP dispositions for updates.
